source.title: What Lies Beneath
source.summary: The resource curse, Dutch disease, critical minerals, and the Islamic concept of communal resource ownership.
source.author: Islamic Economics
source.body_text: Countries that discover oil or minerals often end up worse off, not better. The resource curse is one of the most robust findings in development economics: resource wealth weakens institutions, concentrates power, and crowds out productive sectors through Dutch disease. This episode covers the mechanism, the evidence, and the exceptions (Norway, Botswana). Then it turns to Islamic resource economics: the fay' principle that communal resources belong to the community, the hima system of protected commons, and how sovereign wealth funds (particularly the Gulf model) represent a partial modern application. Pakistan's critical minerals reserves make this directly relevant. The honest assessment: Islamic principles point in the right direction, but no Muslim-majority resource economy has fully solved the institutional challenge.

linkedin.post: One of development economics' most robust findings: countries that discover oil or minerals often end up worse off, not better. The resource curse weakens institutions, concentrates power, and triggers Dutch disease—where resource wealth crowds out productive sectors. Norway and Botswana are rare exceptions. Islamic economics anticipated this challenge. The fay' principle establishes that communal resources belong to the community, not rulers. The hima system created frameworks for protecting commons from overexploitation. Gulf sovereign wealth funds represent a partial modern application of these principles, channeling resource wealth for broader benefit. Yet no Muslim-majority resource economy has fully implemented Islamic resource governance. With Pakistan sitting on significant critical minerals reserves, these questions move from academic to urgent. Listen: https://islamiceconomics.github.io/podcast.html#ep-trt-4

short_video.title: Why Oil Makes Countries Poorer
short_video.hook: Oil should make countries rich. Instead, it usually makes them poorer.
short_video.voiceover: Countries that discover oil often end up worse off, not better. It's called the resource curse. Resource wealth weakens institutions and triggers Dutch disease, where oil money crowds out productive industries. Norway and Botswana are rare exceptions. Islamic economics understood this centuries ago. The fay' principle says communal resources belong to the community, not rulers. Gulf sovereign wealth funds partially apply this idea today. Pakistan sits on critical minerals reserves. The governance model they choose will determine whether they follow the curse or break it.
